title: Foundations of Software Architecture
description: What software architecture is, why it matters, the two values of software, and the paradigms and style vocabulary architects work with.

learning_objectives.text: By the end of this topic, you will be able to explain what software architecture is and why structure is as valuable as behaviour.

children.title: Design, Architecture, and the Two Values
children.description: Design vs architecture, and the tension between behaviour and structure as the two values every system delivers.

learning_objectives.text: Explain why the distinction between design and architecture is artificial — both form a continuous fabric of decisions.
Compare the two values of software (behaviour and structure) and justify why structure is the greater value over time.
Identify the symptoms of a system whose architecture has been neglected in favour of feature delivery.

children.title: What Good Architecture Enables
children.description: Architecture's purpose: facilitating development, deployment, operation, and maintenance while keeping options open.

learning_objectives.text: List the four activities good architecture must facilitate: development, deployment, operation, and maintenance.
Explain why 'keeping options open' — deferring decisions about details — is the core strategy of good architecture.
Describe how team size changes the architectural pressure on a codebase.

children.title: Programming Paradigms
children.description: How structured, object-oriented, and functional programming each remove a capability and what that discipline buys architects.

learning_objectives.text: Summarize how each major paradigm imposes discipline by removing a programming capability.

children.title: Structured and Object-Oriented Programming
children.description: Structured programming's testability argument and OO's real architectural gift: safe polymorphism enabling dependency inversion.

learning_objectives.text: Explain why tests can prove a program wrong but never prove it correct, and what that means for falsifiable units.
Assess the claims that OO 'gave us' encapsulation, inheritance, and polymorphism, identifying which one matters architecturally.
Describe how polymorphism lets a dependency point against the flow of control (dependency inversion).

source_sections: OO gave us Polymorphism? (sort of, but it made it safe to use)
Dependency Inversion (this is the important thing)

children.title: Functional Programming and Immutability
children.description: Immutability as discipline over assignment, and the practical compromises: segregating mutable components and event sourcing.

learning_objectives.text: Explain why race conditions, deadlocks, and concurrency problems disappear in the absence of mutable state.
Describe the two practical compromises to full immutability: segregation of mutable components and event sourcing.

source_sections: Compromise 1: Segregation of mutable and immutable components

children.title: A Tour of Architecture Styles
children.description: The catalog of architecture styles — N-tier, Web-Queue-Worker, microservices, event-driven, big data, big compute — and styles as constraints.

learning_objectives.text: Name the major architecture styles and the workload each is suited for.
Explain how an architecture style acts as a set of constraints that shape a design and create an opinionated 'grain'.
Given a workload description, choose a candidate architecture style and defend the choice in terms of its benefits and challenges.

source_sections: A quick tour of the styles

title: Design Principles
description: The mid-level principles for arranging code: general architectural principles, SOLID, and the component cohesion/coupling principles.

learning_objectives.text: By the end of this topic, you will be able to apply SOLID and component principles when organizing classes, modules, and components.

children.title: General Architectural Principles
children.description: Separation of concerns, encapsulation, dependency inversion, explicit dependencies, single responsibility, DRY, persistence ignorance, and bounded contexts.

learning_objectives.text: Define separation of concerns, encapsulation, DRY, persistence ignorance, and bounded contexts.
Explain how the explicit dependencies principle makes classes honest about their collaborators.
Identify violations of these principles in a described codebase and propose corrections.

children.title: The SOLID Principles at a Glance
children.description: What SOLID is for — arranging functions and data into modules and defining their interconnections — and the executive summary of all five principles.

learning_objectives.text: List the five SOLID principles and state each in one sentence.
Explain at which level (class/module vs component vs architecture) SOLID applies.

children.title: The Single Responsibility Principle
children.description: A module should be responsible to one and only one actor — violation symptoms (accidental duplication, merge conflicts) and remedies.

learning_objectives.text: State the SRP in terms of actors rather than 'doing one thing'.
Diagnose accidental duplication and merge-conflict symptoms as SRP violations.
Apply the facade-based refactorings that separate methods serving different actors.

source_sections: Violation of SRP Symptom 1: Accidental duplication
Violation of SRP Symptom 2: Merge Conflicts
Approach 1: Separate all Methods from Data and Introduce a Facade

children.title: The Open-Closed Principle
children.description: Systems should be open for extension but closed for modification — achieved by separating change reasons into components and protecting by level.

learning_objectives.text: State the OCP and explain its goal: making behaviour extensible without modifying existing code.
Explain how component separation, a protection hierarchy, and dependency inversion together enforce the OCP.
Apply the OCP to a described change scenario by proposing which components should be protected from which.

source_sections: Idea 1: Separate things that should change for different reasons into `components`
Idea 2: Create a hierarchy of protection based on the level of the component
Idea 3: Use dependency inversion to enforce the hierarchy and ensure unidirectional boundaries

children.title: Liskov Substitution and Interface Segregation
children.description: Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types, and clients should not depend on things they don't use — at language and architecture level.

learning_objectives.text: Recognize LSP violations from their symptoms (type-checking conditionals, surprising subtype behaviour).
Explain why ISP matters more in statically typed languages and what it means at the architectural level.
Explain the general wisdom of not depending on things that carry baggage you don't need.

source_sections: ISP at the programming language level

children.title: The Dependency Inversion Principle
children.description: Depend on abstractions, not volatile concretions — coding practices and the abstract factory pattern for managing unavoidable concrete creation.

learning_objectives.text: State the DIP and distinguish volatile concrete classes from stable ones it's safe to depend on.
Apply abstract factories to keep source-code dependencies pointing at abstractions when instances must be created.

source_sections: Coding practice 1: Don't refer to volatile concrete classes

children.title: Component Principles
children.description: SOLID's bigger sibling: which classes belong together in a component (cohesion) and how components may depend on each other (coupling).

learning_objectives.text: Distinguish component cohesion questions from component coupling questions.

children.title: Component Cohesion
children.description: REP, CCP, and CRP, and the tension diagram showing why you can't fully satisfy all three at once.

learning_objectives.text: Define the REP, CCP, and CRP cohesion principles.
Explain the tension diagram and how the balance between cohesion principles shifts as a project matures.
Decide which cohesion principle to favour for a project at a given maturity stage.

source_sections: The Tension Diagram For Component Cohesion

children.title: Component Coupling and Stability
children.description: Acyclic dependencies, breaking cycles, and the stable dependencies / stable abstractions principles with their metrics.

learning_objectives.text: Detect a dependency cycle between components and break it using dependency inversion or a new component.
Compute component stability from fan-in/fan-out and explain why dependencies should point toward stability.
Explain the SAP: stable components should be abstract so they can be extended without modification.

source_sections: Top-Down Design: The develop-ability VS logical
Measuring Abstraction and The Main Sequence

title: Clean Architecture
description: Layers, boundaries, the Dependency Rule, and the Clean Architecture pattern — including how to apply it in a web application and organize the code.

learning_objectives.text: By the end of this topic, you will be able to design a system around the Dependency Rule with business rules independent of frameworks, UI, and databases.

children.title: Layers and Decoupling
children.description: Vertical and horizontal layers, independence dimensions, the fear-of-duplication trap, and decoupling modes from source level to services.

learning_objectives.text: Differentiate horizontal layers from vertical slices and what independence each provides.
Compare source-level, deployment-level, and service-level decoupling modes and their costs.
Explain why defaulting to microservices is a pitfall and describe the recommended decoupling-mode progression.

source_sections: Vertical and Horizontal Layers and Independence
The pitfall of micro-services by default
Uncle Bob's Preferred Decoupling Mode Strategy

children.title: Boundaries
children.description: Where to draw architectural lines, what crossing a boundary means physically, and when partial boundaries are the right trade-off.

learning_objectives.text: Decide where to draw boundary lines between core business rules and details.

children.title: Drawing Boundary Lines
children.description: Boundaries between business rules and the database/GUI, and the plugin architecture as Clean Architecture's foundational idea.

learning_objectives.text: Explain why the database and the GUI are plugins to the business rules, not the other way around.
Apply the plugin-architecture idea to position a new subsystem on the right side of a boundary.

source_sections: Which lines do you draw, and when do you draw them?
The relationship between the database and the business rules
The role of the GUI in the system
The Plugin Architecture - The Foundational Idea of Clean Architecture

children.title: Boundary Anatomy
children.description: What boundary crossings look like at runtime: monolith function calls, threads, local processes, and services.

learning_objectives.text: Describe the mechanics of boundary crossings in monoliths, across threads, local processes, and services.
Classify a given runtime separation (thread, process, service) by the strength of the boundary it creates.

children.title: Partial Boundaries and Their Costs
children.description: Three ways to build a cheaper, partial boundary and the trade-off between implementing and ignoring boundaries.

learning_objectives.text: Describe the three partial-boundary strategies: source-level decoupling, grouped interfaces, and facades.
Weigh the cost of implementing a full boundary against the risk of ignoring it for a given subsystem.

source_sections: Partial Boundary 1: Use Source Level Decoupling Mode
Partial Boundary 2: Group Service Interfaces or Implementations
Partial Boundary 3: Reduce Cognitive Load Introducing a Facade
The Cost of Implementing VS Ignoring Boundaries

children.title: Policy, Level, and Business Rules
children.description: Policies and their levels, entities vs use cases, request/response models, and architectures that scream their domain.

learning_objectives.text: Define 'level' as distance from inputs/outputs and explain why higher-level policy should not depend on lower-level detail.
Distinguish entities (application-independent rules) from use cases (application-specific rules).
Explain what a 'screaming architecture' reveals about a system's intent and why frameworks should not dominate the top-level structure.

children.title: The Clean Architecture Pattern
children.description: The concentric-circle model, the Dependency Rule, crossing boundaries with the Humble Object pattern, and a worked web example.

learning_objectives.text: Apply the Dependency Rule to keep all source-code dependencies pointing inward toward higher-level policy.

children.title: The Dependency Rule and the Four Layers
children.description: Entities, use cases, interface adapters, and frameworks & drivers — and the rule that all dependencies point inward.

learning_objectives.text: Name the four layers of the Clean Architecture and what belongs in each.
Apply the Dependency Rule to decide whether a proposed dependency between two classes is legal.
Explain why the layer count is not fixed at four as long as the Dependency Rule holds.

source_sections: Can I use more than four layers?

children.title: Crossing Boundaries in Practice
children.description: What data crosses boundaries, the Humble Object pattern, presenters and view models, and where ORMs and external-service calls live.

learning_objectives.text: Explain why simple data structures, not entities or database rows, should cross architectural boundaries.
Apply the Humble Object pattern to split hard-to-test behaviour from testable logic at a boundary.
Place data mappers, ORMs, and external-service calls in the correct Clean Architecture layer.

source_sections: More on Presenters and View Models and Views
Where do Data Mappers and ORMs go?
Where do calls to external services go?

children.title: A Clean Web Application Example
children.description: When to use (and not use) the Clean Architecture, a worked web example with controller, use case, and presenter, and the Main component.

learning_objectives.text: Decide whether the Clean Architecture is warranted for a given project profile.
Trace a web request through controller, use-case input port, interactor, output port, and presenter.
Explain the role of Main as the ultimate detail and lowest-level component that wires everything together.

source_sections: When should I use and not use the Clean Architecture?
The Use Case and the Use Case Input and Output Ports
The Presenter and The View Model
The Main Component, The Ultimate Detail

children.title: Details: Database, Web, and Frameworks
children.description: Why the database, the web, and frameworks are details to be kept at arm's length — and how to use frameworks without marrying them.

learning_objectives.text: Argue why the database schema and the web delivery mechanism are details, not the architecture.
Describe the asymmetric-marriage risk of frameworks and strategies to use them while limiting coupling.
Identify the framework marriages that are practically unavoidable and how to contain them.

source_sections: The risks of marrying into a framework
Use frameworks but do not marry them

children.title: Organizing Code
children.description: Concrete packaging strategies — by layer, by feature, ports and adapters, by component — and a component-design case study.

learning_objectives.text: Choose a packaging strategy appropriate to a team's enforcement and encapsulation needs.

children.title: Packaging Strategies
children.description: Package by layer, by feature, ports and adapters, and package by component — trade-offs between organization and encapsulation.

learning_objectives.text: Compare the four packaging strategies and what architectural violations each can or cannot prevent.
Explain how compiler-enforced visibility (rather than convention) keeps an architecture intact.

source_sections: The missing chapter - Actual implementation details of an architecture
Strategy 4: Simon Brown's Package by Component
More on the strategies: Organization VS Encapsulation

children.title: Case Study: Video Sales
children.description: Uncle Bob's worked example: use-case analysis, preliminary component architecture, and dependency-management verification.

learning_objectives.text: Apply the three-step method: identify actors and use cases, sketch a component architecture, verify dependencies.
Verify that a proposed component diagram respects the Dependency Rule and points toward stability.

source_sections: Step 1: Use Case Analysis: Identify the actors and their use cases
Step 2: Create a Preliminary Component Architecture

children.title: Clean Architecture in ASP.NET Core
children.description: Microsoft's rendition of the onion: Application Core, Infrastructure, and UI projects, and which types belong in each.

learning_objectives.text: Map Clean Architecture layers onto an ASP.NET Core solution's Application Core, Infrastructure, and UI projects.
Classify a given type (entity, interface, EF DbContext, controller, view model) into the correct project.

title: Architecture Styles in Practice
description: Monoliths, layered N-tier systems, containers, Web-Queue-Worker, and event-driven architecture — the styles most web systems are built from.

learning_objectives.text: By the end of this topic, you will be able to select and justify an architecture style for a typical web workload.

children.title: Monoliths and Layered Applications
children.description: All-in-one applications, what layers buy you, and the traditional N-layer architecture with its limits.

learning_objectives.text: Define a monolithic application and describe when single-project, all-in-one apps are appropriate.
Explain the benefits and costs of logical layering (UI, business logic, data access) inside a single deployment unit.
Analyze the dependency problem of traditional N-layer designs where business logic depends on data access.

children.title: Monoliths in Containers
children.description: Deploying a monolith as a container: Docker support, scaling out container instances, and common troubleshooting.

learning_objectives.text: Explain how containerizing a monolith changes deployment and horizontal scaling without changing the architecture.
Describe the Docker development workflow for a web app and common port/certificate troubleshooting steps.

source_sections: Monolithic application deployed as a container

children.title: N-Tier Architecture Style
children.description: Physical tiers, closed vs open layer access, when N-tier fits, and best practices for running it on VMs.

learning_objectives.text: Distinguish logical layers from physical tiers and explain closed-layer vs open-layer designs.
List the scenarios where N-tier remains the right choice (lift-and-shift, heterogeneous platforms, simple web apps).
Evaluate an N-tier deployment against its best practices (load balancing, caching, autoscaling, async messaging).

source_sections: N-tier architecture style: When to use this architecture
N-tier architecture on VMs: Other considerations

children.title: Web-Queue-Worker Style
children.description: A web front end plus a message queue plus a background worker — the simplest cloud-native step beyond a pure monolith.

learning_objectives.text: Describe the Web-Queue-Worker style and the role the queue plays in decoupling front end from background work.
Identify workloads where Web-Queue-Worker is a better fit than microservices.
Apply the style's best practices: stateless web tier, idempotent workers, polyglot persistence kept simple.

source_sections: Web-Queue-Worker architecture style: When to use this architecture
Web-Queue-Worker on App Service: Other considerations

children.title: Event-Driven Architecture Style
children.description: Producers, consumers, pub/sub vs event streaming, consumer patterns, and the hard parts: ordering, idempotency, and delivery guarantees.

learning_objectives.text: Differentiate pub/sub messaging from event streaming and the consumer patterns each supports.
Identify when event-driven architecture fits: high volume, real-time processing, decoupled producers and consumers.
Explain the delivery-guarantee challenges (at-least-once, ordering, duplicates) and how consumers must compensate.

source_sections: Event-driven architecture style: When to use this architecture

title: Web Application Architecture
description: Architecting modern web applications: characteristics, front-end choices (traditional vs SPA), server-side patterns, security, data access, and testing — with ASP.NET Core as the concrete stack.

learning_objectives.text: By the end of this topic, you will be able to architect a maintainable, testable web application from the front end through data access.

children.title: Modern Web App Characteristics
children.description: What 'modern' means: cloud-hosted, cross-platform, modular, testable, supporting both traditional and SPA behaviours.

learning_objectives.text: List the characteristics of modern web applications and why each matters for maintainability and scale.
Explain how modularity and loose coupling make a web app easier to test and evolve.

source_sections: Characteristics of Modern Web Applications: Blazor

children.title: Front-End Architecture
children.description: Choosing between server-rendered apps and SPAs, and the client-side technology landscape from HTML/CSS/JS to SPA frameworks.

learning_objectives.text: Choose between a traditional web app, a SPA, or a hybrid based on team skills and UX requirements.

children.title: Traditional Web Apps vs SPAs
children.description: The decision between server-rendered apps, single-page applications, and Blazor, with a decision table.

learning_objectives.text: State the conditions favouring traditional web apps (simple client requirements, no-JS support, SEO) vs SPAs (rich UX, exposed API).
Use the decision table to recommend traditional, SPA, or Blazor for a described product.
Explain the staffing and tooling costs a SPA adds to a project.

source_sections: Choose Between Traditional Web Apps and Single Page Apps (SPAs)
Choose Between Traditional Web Apps and Single Page Apps (SPAs): Blazor
When to choose traditional web apps

children.title: Client-Side Web Technologies
children.description: HTML, CSS and preprocessors, JavaScript, and the role of jQuery versus modern SPA frameworks.

learning_objectives.text: Describe the responsibilities of HTML, CSS, and JavaScript in a web client and what CSS preprocessors add.
Compare jQuery's DOM-centric model with a SPA framework's data-binding model.

children.title: SPA Frameworks
children.description: Angular, React, Vue, and Blazor WebAssembly — and how to choose among them, including data flow to WebAssembly clients.

learning_objectives.text: Summarize the architectural models of Angular, React, Vue, and Blazor WebAssembly.
Choose a SPA framework using criteria like team experience, ecosystem maturity, and tooling.
Describe how a Blazor WebAssembly client obtains data through web APIs.

source_sections: Getting data to Blazor WebAssembly apps

children.title: Server-Side Application Patterns
children.description: MVC and Razor Pages, dependency injection, application structuring, cross-cutting concerns, and security in ASP.NET Core.

learning_objectives.text: Structure a server-side web application with clear request mapping, explicit dependencies, and centralized cross-cutting concerns.

children.title: MVC and Razor Pages
children.description: Page-based vs controller-based models, routing requests to responses, thin controllers, and real-time client communication.

learning_objectives.text: Decide between Razor Pages and MVC controllers for a given application's page and API mix.
Explain routing, model binding, model validation, and filters in the request pipeline.
Apply techniques for keeping controllers thin (mediator-style handlers, pushing logic into services).

children.title: Dependency Injection and Application Structure
children.description: Declaring dependencies, configuring services, feature-based organization, and handling cross-cutting concerns.

learning_objectives.text: Configure constructor-injected services and explain why explicit dependencies improve testability.
Organize an application by feature folders or areas instead of technical file types.
Identify cross-cutting concerns (logging, caching, validation) and address them with filters or decorators rather than duplication.

children.title: Web Application Security
children.description: Identity management, authentication (including external providers), authorization with roles and claims, and securing web APIs.

learning_objectives.text: Differentiate authentication from authorization and describe where each happens in the request pipeline.
Apply claims- and role-based authorization to protect pages, actions, and APIs.
Explain how token-based authentication secures APIs consumed by SPAs and mobile clients.

children.title: Data Access
children.description: EF Core patterns, choosing relational vs NoSQL stores, and caching data within the application.

learning_objectives.text: Design a data-access layer that encapsulates persistence behind abstractions and matches the store to the workload.

children.title: Entity Framework Core Patterns
children.description: DbContext lifetime, configuration, fetching and storing data, loading related data, encapsulation with repositories, and resilient connections.

learning_objectives.text: Explain DbContext scoping and why request-scoped contexts suit web applications.
Compare eager, explicit, and lazy loading of related data and their pitfalls in web apps.
Encapsulate data access behind repository-style abstractions with connection resiliency for transient failures.

source_sections: Working with Data in ASP.NET Core Apps
Execution strategies and explicit transactions using BeginTransaction and multiple DbContexts

children.title: Choosing a Data Store
children.description: Full ORM vs micro-ORM, the SQL vs NoSQL decision from two perspectives, and the NoSQL store taxonomy.

learning_objectives.text: Weigh EF Core against a micro-ORM like Dapper on productivity vs performance.
Classify NoSQL stores (key-value, document, wide-column, graph) and the access patterns each optimizes.
Recommend SQL, NoSQL, or a hybrid for a workload based on consistency, schema, and scale needs.

children.title: Application-Level Caching
children.description: Response caching and data caching in the web application tier, with cache keys, expiration, and invalidation.

learning_objectives.text: Differentiate response caching from data caching and where each applies in a web app.
Implement cache-aside data caching with sensible keys, durations, and invalidation on updates.

children.title: Testing
children.description: The testing pyramid, the architectural test boundary, and writing unit, integration, and functional tests for web apps.

learning_objectives.text: Design a test strategy that covers business logic with unit tests and critical paths with integration and functional tests.

children.title: Testing Strategy and the Test Boundary
children.description: Kinds of automated tests, the testing pyramid, what to test, and tests as an architectural boundary with design-for-testability.

learning_objectives.text: Distinguish unit, integration, and functional tests and the failure modes each catches.
Explain the testing pyramid and why over-investing in UI tests is fragile.
Explain why tests are part of the system and how structural coupling to internals makes them brittle.

children.title: Writing and Organizing Tests
children.description: Organizing test projects, naming conventions, and concrete unit/integration/functional testing of ASP.NET Core apps.

learning_objectives.text: Organize test projects to mirror production code and name tests so failures explain themselves.
Write an integration test against a real database and a functional test against the app's HTTP surface using a test host.

title: API Design and Integration
description: HTTP fundamentals, RESTful API design, versioning, implementation practices for robust APIs, and operating published APIs.

learning_objectives.text: By the end of this topic, you will be able to design and implement a well-behaved, versioned, documented web API.

children.title: HTTP and Web Protocols
children.description: HTTP request/response semantics, TCP vs UDP, and RPC vs REST as API paradigms.

learning_objectives.text: Describe HTTP's request/response model, methods, and status-code classes.
Compare TCP and UDP guarantees and when each transport fits.
Contrast RPC's behaviour-centric calls with REST's resource-centric design and pick the right paradigm for a use case.

children.title: RESTful API Design
children.description: Designing resources, URIs, and method semantics; pagination, HATEOAS, OpenAPI; and versioning an evolving API.

learning_objectives.text: Design a resource-oriented API with correct HTTP method semantics and an explicit versioning strategy.

children.title: Resources and URIs
children.description: Platform-independent resource modelling and URI naming conventions oriented around nouns, collections, and relationships.

learning_objectives.text: Model an API around resources and collections rather than operations.
Apply URI naming conventions: plural nouns, shallow nesting, no verbs.

source_sections: Best practices for RESTful web API design
Define RESTful web API resource URIs

children.title: HTTP Methods and Semantics
children.description: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE semantics, idempotency expectations, and resource MIME types.

learning_objectives.text: Select the correct HTTP method and status codes for create, replace, partial-update, and delete operations.
Explain PATCH semantics (JSON merge patch vs JSON patch) and when PATCH beats PUT.
Use media types and content negotiation to version and shape representations.

children.title: Advanced API Capabilities
children.description: Async methods returning 202, pagination and filtering, partial responses, HATEOAS, the maturity model, and OpenAPI.

learning_objectives.text: Implement pagination, filtering, and partial responses for large collections and binary resources.
Explain HATEOAS and the Richardson maturity model's levels.
Document an API contract with OpenAPI definitions.

children.title: API Versioning
children.description: No versioning, URI, query-string, header, and media-type versioning — trade-offs for clients, caches, and HATEOAS.

learning_objectives.text: Compare the four explicit versioning mechanisms and their effects on caching and client code.
Choose a versioning strategy for a public API and justify it against breaking-change policy.

children.title: Multitenancy and Tracing
children.description: Tenant isolation via subdomains, headers, or URI paths, and propagating distributed trace context through APIs.

learning_objectives.text: Compare DNS-level, header-based, and URI-path tenancy models for multitenant APIs.
Explain W3C trace-context propagation and why APIs should forward correlation identifiers.

source_sections: Use subdomain or domain-based isolation (DNS-level tenancy)
Pass tenant-specific information through the URI path
Enable distributed tracing and trace context in APIs

children.title: Web API Implementation
children.description: Implementing APIs that honour HTTP: idempotent processing, exception handling, ETags, large payloads, long-running work, and API operations.

learning_objectives.text: Implement an API that is idempotent where required, fails informatively, and stays responsive under large or slow operations.

children.title: Request Processing Practices
children.description: Idempotency rules per method, avoiding chatty operations, honouring the HTTP spec in responses, content negotiation, and HATEOAS links.

learning_objectives.text: Implement handlers that keep GET/PUT/DELETE idempotent and POST free of unrelated side effects.
Explain how content negotiation selects representations and what the Accept/Content-Type headers promise.
Refactor a chatty API surface into coarser-grained operations.

source_sections: GET, PUT, DELETE, HEAD, and PATCH actions should be idempotent
POST actions that create new resources should not have unrelated side-effects
Avoid implementing chatty POST, PUT, and DELETE operations
Follow the HTTP specification when sending a response
Provide links to support HATEOAS-style navigation and discovery of resources

children.title: Exceptions, Caching, and Concurrency
children.description: Returning meaningful errors, distinguishing client from server faults, HTTP caching with Cache-Control, and ETags for queries and optimistic concurrency.

learning_objectives.text: Map exceptions to appropriate 4xx/5xx responses with consistent logging.
Implement client-side caching with Cache-Control and validate with ETags to avoid re-sending unchanged data.
Implement optimistic concurrency using ETags and If-Match to prevent lost updates.

source_sections: Capture exceptions and return a meaningful response to clients
Handle exceptions consistently and log information about errors
Distinguish between client-side errors and server-side errors
Provide ETags to optimize query processing
Use ETags to Support Optimistic Concurrency

children.title: Large Payloads and Long-Running Work
children.description: Streaming and chunking large objects, partial GETs with ranges, 100-Continue handling, pagination, async 202 patterns, and stateless requests.

learning_objectives.text: Implement HEAD-plus-range partial retrieval for large binary resources.
Implement the 202 Accepted + status-endpoint pattern for long-running operations.
Explain why statelessness is a precondition for horizontal API scaling.

source_sections: Optimize requests and responses that involve large objects
Implement partial responses for clients that don't support asynchronous operations
Avoid sending unnecessary 100-Continue status messages in client applications
Support pagination for requests that might return large numbers of objects
Provide asynchronous support for long-running requests
Ensure that each request is stateless

children.title: Protecting and Operating APIs
children.description: Throttling against abuse, connection management, publishing, testing, documenting, client SDKs, and monitoring a web API.

learning_objectives.text: Implement client tracking and throttling to protect an API from overload and DoS.
Plan the operational surface of a published API: docs, SDKs, testing, and monitoring.

source_sections: Track clients and implement throttling to reduce the chances of DoS attacks
Publishing and managing a web API
Document the REST operations for a web API

title: Scalability and Distributed Systems
description: The building blocks of scalable systems: CAP and consistency, availability, DNS/CDN/load balancing, database scaling and partitioning, caching, async work, and autoscaling.

learning_objectives.text: By the end of this topic, you will be able to scale a web system by combining edge infrastructure, database scaling, caching, and asynchronous work.

children.title: Scalability Fundamentals
children.description: Performance vs scalability, latency vs throughput, the CAP theorem, and consistency/availability patterns.

learning_objectives.text: Reason about distributed-system trade-offs using CAP and consistency models.

children.title: Performance, Scalability, and CAP
children.description: Definitions of performance vs scalability and latency vs throughput, the CAP theorem, and weak/eventual/strong consistency.

learning_objectives.text: Distinguish a performance problem from a scalability problem and latency from throughput.
Apply the CAP theorem to classify a data store as CP or AP for a given failure scenario.
Match weak, eventual, and strong consistency models to appropriate use cases.

children.title: Availability Patterns
children.description: Active-passive and active-active fail-over, availability arithmetic in 9s, and availability in sequence vs in parallel.

learning_objectives.text: Compare active-passive and active-active fail-over including their data-loss risks.
Calculate composite availability for components in sequence and in parallel.
Translate 99.9% and 99.99% availability into acceptable downtime per year.

source_sections: Availability in parallel vs in sequence

children.title: Traffic and Edge Infrastructure
children.description: DNS, content delivery networks, load balancers, and reverse proxies — getting requests to healthy servers fast.

learning_objectives.text: Design the edge path of a web system from DNS resolution through CDN and load balancer to origin.

children.title: DNS and Content Delivery
children.description: How DNS routing works, push vs pull CDNs, and the trade-offs of serving content from the edge.

learning_objectives.text: Describe DNS resolution and routing methods (weighted, latency-based, geolocation).
Choose between push and pull CDN strategies for sites with different traffic patterns.

children.title: CDN Best Practices
children.description: Operating CDNs: challenges, deployment of static assets, routing and versioning, cache control, securing edge content, and fallback.

learning_objectives.text: Plan cache-control and versioning policies so deployments don't serve stale assets.
Design a CDN fallback path for origin failures and explain edge security controls.

source_sections: How and why a CDN is used

children.title: Load Balancers and Reverse Proxies
children.description: Layer 4 vs layer 7 load balancing, horizontal scaling implications, and load balancers vs reverse proxies.

learning_objectives.text: Compare layer 4 and layer 7 load balancing and what each can route on.
Explain the statelessness and session implications of scaling out behind a load balancer.
Differentiate the roles of a load balancer and a reverse proxy and when to deploy each.

children.title: Database Scaling
children.description: Scaling the data tier: replication, federation, sharding, denormalization, SQL tuning, and designing partitions deliberately.

learning_objectives.text: Select and combine replication, sharding, and partitioning strategies for a growing dataset.

children.title: Replication and Federation
children.description: Master-slave and master-master replication with their failure modes, and functional federation of databases.

learning_objectives.text: Compare master-slave and master-master replication including consistency and fail-over trade-offs.
Explain replication lag and the data-loss window it creates.
Describe federation by function and the join/complexity costs it introduces.

children.title: Sharding, Denormalization, and SQL Tuning
children.description: Sharding data across machines, denormalizing to avoid expensive joins, and core SQL tuning techniques.

learning_objectives.text: Design a sharding scheme and identify its rebalancing and hot-spot risks.
Decide when denormalization's read benefits outweigh its write and consistency costs.
Apply schema tightening and indexing to address slow queries.

children.title: Designing Data Partitions
children.description: Horizontal, vertical, and functional partitioning, and designing partitions for scalability, query performance, and availability.

learning_objectives.text: Differentiate horizontal, vertical, and functional partitioning and combine them where appropriate.
Choose a partition key that balances load and avoids hot partitions.
Design partitions so the most critical data is the most available.

children.title: Operating Partitioned Systems
children.description: Application design considerations for partitioned data and rebalancing partitions offline or online.

learning_objectives.text: Explain how partitioning changes application code: routing, cross-partition queries, and transactions.
Compare offline and online partition-rebalancing migrations and their availability impact.

children.title: Caching
children.description: Cache placement across the stack, update patterns, and running shared caches correctly: expiration, invalidation, concurrency, and consistency.

learning_objectives.text: Design a multi-level caching strategy with explicit update, expiration, and invalidation policies.

children.title: Cache Layers
children.description: Caching at the client, CDN, web server, database, and application levels, including query-level vs object-level caching.

learning_objectives.text: Map the cache locations available in a web stack and what each can serve.
Choose between query-level and object-level application caching for given access patterns.

source_sections: Caching at the database query level

children.title: Cache Update Patterns
children.description: Cache-aside, write-through, write-behind, and refresh-ahead — mechanics, advantages, and failure modes of each.

learning_objectives.text: Implement cache-aside and explain its stale-data window.
Compare write-through, write-behind, and refresh-ahead on latency, durability, and complexity.
Select an update pattern for a workload given its read/write mix and consistency tolerance.

children.title: Distributed Caching in Practice
children.description: Private vs shared caches, deciding what and when to cache, caching dynamic data, and caching effectively at scale.

learning_objectives.text: Differentiate private and shared caching and the consistency implications of each.
Decide which data is worth caching based on volatility, access frequency, and reconstruction cost.

source_sections: Determine how to cache data effectively

children.title: Cache Consistency and Protection
children.description: Expiration policy, client-side invalidation, concurrent updates (optimistic vs pessimistic), high availability, eventual consistency, and protecting cached data.

learning_objectives.text: Set expiration policies that balance staleness against cache effectiveness.
Handle concurrent cache updates with optimistic or pessimistic approaches as appropriate.
Explain how caching interacts with eventual consistency and what data protection a shared cache needs.

source_sections: Manage data expiration in a cache
Invalidate data in a client-side cache
Implement high availability and scalability, and improve performance

children.title: Asynchronous Work
children.description: Message queues, task queues, back pressure, and designing reliable background jobs.

learning_objectives.text: Move slow or bursty work off the request path using queues and well-designed background jobs.

children.title: Message and Task Queues
children.description: Queues as buffers between producers and workers, task queues, and back pressure when queues grow.

learning_objectives.text: Explain how message queues decouple producers from consumers and smooth bursty load.
Apply back pressure when queue depth signals that the system is saturated.

children.title: Background Job Design
children.description: Job types, event-driven vs schedule-driven triggers, returning results to callers, and designing for idempotency.

learning_objectives.text: Choose event-driven or schedule-driven triggers for a background task.
Design a result-reporting path so callers learn the outcome of asynchronous work.
Design idempotent job handlers that tolerate at-least-once execution.

children.title: Background Job Coordination and Reliability
children.description: Partitioning job workloads, resolving conflicts, coordinating multi-instance workers, and reliability, security, observability, and scaling concerns.

learning_objectives.text: Coordinate multiple worker instances safely using leases, locks, or queue semantics.
Analyze a background-job design for reliability gaps: poison messages, retries, and partial failures.

children.title: Autoscaling
children.description: Scaling out automatically: components of an autoscaling system and the application-design considerations that make scaling safe.

learning_objectives.text: Describe the components of an autoscaling loop: instrumentation, decision logic, and scaling actions.
Identify application-design prerequisites for safe scale-in/scale-out (statelessness, graceful shutdown, queue-length signals).
Choose scaling metrics beyond CPU — queue depth, custom business counters — for a given workload.

title: Microservices
description: Designing microservices: the style and its critics, domain-driven decomposition, interservice communication, gateways, APIs, data ownership, and orchestration.

learning_objectives.text: By the end of this topic, you will be able to decompose a domain into microservices and design their communication, APIs, and data ownership.

children.title: Microservices Architecture Style
children.description: What microservices are, the supporting components, benefits, challenges, best practices, and antipatterns.

learning_objectives.text: Define the characteristics of a microservice: small, independently deployable, owning its data.
Weigh the benefits (independent deployment, fault isolation) against the challenges (complexity, data integrity, network congestion).
Recognize microservices antipatterns such as the distributed monolith.

children.title: A Critical View of Services
children.description: Uncle Bob's critique: services are not an architecture by themselves, the decoupling hype, and the functional-decomposition pitfall.

learning_objectives.text: Explain why splitting into services does not by itself create architectural boundaries.
Critique the claims of total decoupling and independent development used to justify microservices.
Analyze the cross-cutting-change weakness of services decomposed purely by function, and the vertical-layers remedy.

source_sections: The Independence of Development and Deployment Hype
The Pitfall of Services by Functional Decomposition

children.title: Microservices Design Patterns
children.description: The catalog of patterns that address common microservices challenges: ambassador, anti-corruption layer, BFF, bulkhead, sidecar, strangler fig, and more.

learning_objectives.text: Match common microservices design patterns to the problems they solve.
Select supporting patterns (gateway, sidecar, bulkhead) when designing a service deployment.

children.title: Domain-Driven Design
children.description: Decomposing a system the DDD way: strategic domain analysis, tactical patterns, and deriving microservice boundaries.

learning_objectives.text: Derive service boundaries from domain analysis rather than organizational or technical convenience.

children.title: Domain Analysis and Bounded Contexts
children.description: Mapping the business domain, subdomains, and bounded contexts using the drone-delivery scenario.

learning_objectives.text: Analyze a business domain to identify subdomains and their relationships.
Define bounded contexts and explain why models need not be consistent across them.

source_sections: Use domain analysis to model microservices
Use domain analysis to model microservices: Introduction

children.title: Tactical DDD Patterns
children.description: Entities, value objects, aggregates, domain and application services, and domain events — applied to the drone-delivery domain.

learning_objectives.text: Distinguish entities from value objects by identity and mutability.
Design aggregates as consistency boundaries with a single root.
Apply domain events to communicate state changes between aggregates and services.

source_sections: Use tactical DDD to design microservices

children.title: Defining Microservice Boundaries
children.description: From domain model to services: sizing rules, when to split aggregates, and whether DDD is worth applying at all.

learning_objectives.text: Apply the boundary heuristics: a service should be no smaller than an aggregate and no larger than a bounded context.
Evaluate whether the DDD investment is justified for a given project's complexity.

source_sections: Example: Defining microservices for the Drone Delivery application
Domain-driven design – Should you apply it?

children.title: Communication
children.description: How services talk: sync vs async messaging, service meshes, distributed transactions, gateways, and message encoding.

learning_objectives.text: Design the communication fabric of a microservices system, choosing protocols, patterns, and encodings deliberately.

children.title: Interservice Communication
children.description: Synchronous vs asynchronous messaging trade-offs, service meshes, distributed transactions, and service discovery.

learning_objectives.text: Choose between synchronous calls and asynchronous messages for each service interaction.
Explain what a service mesh offloads from application code.
Apply saga-style compensation instead of distributed transactions across services.
Describe service discovery and why dynamic environments need it.

source_sections: Drone Delivery: Choosing the messaging patterns

children.title: API Gateways
children.description: Gateway routing, aggregation, and offloading; deployment options and choosing a gateway technology.

learning_objectives.text: Explain the three gateway functions: routing, aggregation, and offloading.
Choose a gateway approach (reverse proxy, service mesh ingress, managed gateway) for a deployment.

source_sections: How to use an API gateway

children.title: Message Encoding
children.description: Encoding considerations for messages: readability, size, payload understanding, schema versioning, and payload structure.

learning_objectives.text: Identify the encoding requirements of a message exchange: human readability, size, schema evolution.
Plan schema versioning so producers and consumers can evolve independently.

children.title: Choosing Encoding Formats
children.description: JSON, CSV, Protocol Buffers, Avro, Parquet, MessagePack, and CBOR — strengths, library support, and interoperability.

learning_objectives.text: Compare text formats (JSON, CSV) with binary formats (Protobuf, Avro, MessagePack, CBOR) on size, speed, and tooling.
Select an encoding format for a high-throughput interservice exchange and justify it.

children.title: Microservice APIs
children.description: Designing the public and internal APIs of microservices: REST over HTTP, mapping REST to DDD, versioning, and idempotency.

learning_objectives.text: Differentiate public (client-facing) from backend (interservice) API requirements.
Map REST resources and verbs onto DDD aggregates and domain operations.
Design idempotent operations so retried requests cannot corrupt state.

source_sections: Generic data access APIs: OData and GraphQL considerations
When to consider generic data access APIs

children.title: Data Management
children.description: Data ownership per service, polyglot persistence, eventual consistency across services, and the drone-delivery data-store choices.

learning_objectives.text: Explain the database-per-service rule and the integration problems it prevents.
Analyze the consistency challenges of data spread across services and apply patterns to manage them.
Choose appropriate, possibly different, data stores for each service in a described system.

source_sections: Example: Choose data stores for the drone delivery application

children.title: Containers and Orchestration
children.description: Containerized microservices, what an orchestrator does, and the decision factors for choosing a compute platform.

learning_objectives.text: Explain what container orchestration provides: scheduling, scaling, service discovery, and self-healing.
Evaluate compute platforms for microservices against the key decision factors: communication, scaling, deployability, observability, and state.

title: Cloud-Native Operations
description: Running web systems well: the twelve-factor methodology, CI/CD and deployment strategies, resilience to transient faults, and monitoring/observability.

learning_objectives.text: By the end of this topic, you will be able to take a web system from commit to production with safe deployments, fault tolerance, and full observability.

children.title: The Twelve-Factor App
children.description: The twelve factors for building software-as-a-service apps that are portable, scalable, and continuously deployable.

learning_objectives.text: Audit an application against all twelve factors and identify violations.

children.title: Codebase Through Build-Release-Run
children.description: Factors I-V: one codebase many deploys, explicit dependencies, config in the environment, backing services as attached resources, and separated build/release/run stages.

learning_objectives.text: Explain why config belongs in environment variables and what the litmus test for config is.
Treat backing services as attached resources swappable without code changes.
Describe the strict separation of build, release, and run stages and why releases must be immutable.

source_sections: One codebase tracked in revision control, many deploys
Treat backing services as attached resources
Strictly separate build and run stages

children.title: Processes Through Admin Processes
children.description: Factors VI-XII: stateless processes, port binding, scaling via the process model, disposability, dev/prod parity, logs as event streams, and one-off admin processes.

learning_objectives.text: Explain why processes must be stateless and share-nothing, with state in backing services.
Apply fast startup and graceful shutdown to make processes disposable.
Explain logs as event streams written to stdout and why apps should not manage log files.
Keep development, staging, and production as similar as possible and identify the gaps that break parity.

Scale out via the process model
Maximize robustness with fast startup and graceful shutdown
Keep development, staging, and production as similar as possible
Run admin/management tasks as one-off processes

children.title: CI/CD and Deployment
children.description: Continuous integration and delivery for distributed systems, and deployment strategies that release safely.

learning_objectives.text: Design a delivery pipeline that ships independent services safely and frequently.

children.title: CI/CD for Microservices
children.description: Why a robust pipeline matters more with many services, the challenges, and monorepo vs multirepo.

learning_objectives.text: Explain why independent deployability demands per-service pipelines and automated quality gates.
Weigh monorepo against multirepo for a multi-team microservices organization.

source_sections: Why a robust CI/CD pipeline matters

children.title: Deployment Strategies
children.description: Rolling updates, blue-green deployment, canary releases, progressive delivery with GitOps, and deploying web apps.

Select a deployment strategy for a service given its traffic and failure tolerance.

children.title: Resilience
children.description: Handling the transient faults inherent to cloud environments with disciplined retry strategies.

learning_objectives.text: Build fault-handling that retries transient errors safely without amplifying outages.

children.description: Why transient faults occur in the cloud, the challenges they pose, and determining retry counts and intervals.

learning_objectives.text: Explain why shared, commodity cloud infrastructure makes transient faults normal rather than exceptional.
Determine whether an operation is safe to retry and choose an appropriate retry count and backoff.

children.description: Retry antipatterns, testing retry logic, managing policy configuration, logging transient faults, and handling operations that keep failing.

Test and tune retry policies against injected faults before production.

children.title: Monitoring and Observability
children.description: Monitoring scenarios from health to SLA, instrumenting applications, the telemetry pipeline, and turning data into dashboards and alerts.

learning_objectives.text: Design end-to-end observability: scenarios, instrumentation, collection, analysis, and alerting.

children.description: The monitoring scenario landscape, health monitoring with alerts, and availability monitoring with its data needs.

children.title: Performance and Security Monitoring
children.description: Detecting degradation under load, capacity signals, and monitoring for security events and anomalies.

learning_objectives.text: Define performance baselines and detect gradual degradation before users do.
Identify the security signals worth monitoring: failed logins, anomalous access, resource abuse.

children.title: SLA, Usage, and Audit Monitoring
children.description: Proving SLA compliance, auditing regulated operations, and understanding feature usage.

learning_objectives.text: Define the data needed to prove SLA compliance and compute availability against targets.
Explain audit-trail requirements for regulated operations and how usage data informs capacity and product decisions.

children.title: Instrumentation
children.description: The monitoring pipeline, sources of telemetry, and instrumenting applications with correlatable, complete event data.

Information to include in the instrumentation data

children.title: Collecting and Storing Telemetry
children.description: Pull vs push collection, consolidating instrumentation data, storage strategies, retention, and down-sampling.

Plan telemetry storage with rotation, retention, and down-sampling appropriate to each analysis tier.

children.title: Analysis, Dashboards, and Alerting
children.description: Hot, warm, and cold analysis paths, correlating data, troubleshooting, dashboards, alerting, and reporting.

learning_objectives.text: Match hot, warm, and cold analysis paths to incident response, trending, and forensics.
Design dashboards and alert thresholds that surface problems without alert fatigue.
